title: Clauses and Sentence Types: The Architecture of Sentences

questions.question: Which of the following is a CLAUSE (not a phrase)?
questions.rationale: A clause contains a subject and a finite verb ('she was'); a phrase does not. 'Running very fast' has a verb form but no subject, so it is a participial phrase, not a clause.

questions.question: A sentence with one main clause and one subordinate clause is:
questions.rationale: Complex = 1 main + 1 or more subordinate ('When the dog barked, the postman fled'). Compound needs 2 main clauses; compound-complex needs 2 main + 1 subordinate.

questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'Although the offer was generous, she declined it, but she sent a polite note.'
questions.rationale: Main clauses: 'she declined it' and 'she sent a polite note' (2). Subordinate: 'Although the offer was generous' (1). Two main + one subordinate = compound-complex.

questions.question: In 'I know that she left yesterday', the clause 'that she left yesterday' functions as a:
questions.rationale: Replace it with 'it': 'I know it' still works - the clause is the object of the verb, hence a noun clause. Adjective clauses modify nouns; adverb clauses modify verbs answering when/why/if.

questions.question: 'The car that I bought last year is already rusting.' The clause 'that I bought last year' is:
questions.rationale: It tells us WHICH car - restrictive/defining - so it takes no commas and allows 'that'. A non-defining clause would merely add information about an already identified car and would be comma-set and use 'which'.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated CORRECTLY?
options: The rain stopped; we left immediately.
The rain stopped, we left immediately.
The rain stopped we left immediately.
Although the rain stopped, we left immediately however.
questions.rationale: Option 1 joins two main clauses correctly with a semicolon. Option 2 is a comma splice; option 3 is a fused run-on; option 4 mixes subordination with 'however' incorrectly.

questions.question: 'Walking to school, the clock struck nine.' This sentence contains:
questions.rationale: The opening participle has nothing in the main clause to attach to - the clock was not walking to school. Fix: 'Walking to school, I heard the clock strike nine.'

questions.question: 'One of the students who ___ present today will be fined.' The correct verb form is:
questions.rationale: The relative clause attaches to the plural noun 'students' (the students who ARE present), not to 'one'. Agreement questions are usually clause-structure questions in disguise: find the noun the clause actually modifies.

questions.question: 'What a view this is!' is an example of:
questions.rationale: Exclamatory sentences express strong feeling, typically introduced by 'what' or 'how': 'What a view this is!' Interrogative asks; imperative commands; declarative states.

questions.question: Which conjunction set can join two main clauses to form a COMPOUND sentence?
options: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
questions.rationale: Only coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS) or a semicolon can legally join two independent clauses. The other sets are subordinators - they create subordinate clauses, producing complex sentences.
